24 to 63 inches, pale yellow (5Y 7/3) loam, pale olive (5Y 6/3) moist; massive; slightly hard, friable, slightly sticky and plastic; strongly effervescent; a few fine soft masses of lime; a few fine roots; common fine pores.
Texture of the surface layer is loam or silty clay loam. Coarse fragments in the soil range from 0 to 15 percent. Soil color hue is 10YR through 5Y. The Al horizon color range is grayish brown and light brownish gray. The B2 horizon color range is grayish brown and light yellowish brown, light brownish gray and pale brown. The Cca horizon color range is pale yellow, light yellowish brown and pale olive. Lime is segregated in few to common soft masses and threads. Strata of fine sandy loam and clay loam occur below 20 inches in some pedons.
McRae soils are associated with Fort Collins, Thurlow and Thedalund soils. They lack the B2t horizon of the Fort Collins and Thurlow soils. They lack the shale bedrock of the Thedalund soils.
McRae loam, 4 to 8 percent slopes (Ms).
This soil is on footslopes and fans in intermittent and perennial stream valleys. The areas range in size from 15 to 50 acres and in places are dissected by short gullies. Slope gradient increases from 4 percent at the valley bottom to 10 or 12 percent immediately below the residual soils that border the valleys. The soil profile is the typical one described for the series. A few surface gravels are present where gravel terraces border the valleys. Included in the mapping were areas with a silt loam surface.
Surface runoff is medium, and the erosion hazard is moderate. Most areas receive runoff moisture from soils that lie above them.
This soil is suited to irrigated and dryland crops. It is also suited to range. Moisture conservation and erosion control are important problems in managing this soil.
(Capability Unit IIIe-3 Dryland; IIIe-1 Irrigated; Silty range site 10-14 inch precipitation zone; Windbreak Suitability Group 1).
